info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 2.3: AI-Assisted Metadata Enrichment, Entity Extraction, and Validation Auditing.

name.text: 01 Question: Why Anyone Would Let a Machine Catalogue a Manuscript

questiontext.text: Manual cataloguing runs at hours per folio, and archives hold hundreds of thousands of uncatalogued items. What does that make the central question about AI cataloguing?

generalfeedback.text: AI can generate manuscript metadata thousands of times faster than a human, but because it predicts rather than knows, the real skill is measuring and auditing what it produces.

answer.text: Not whether AI can generate metadata, which it plainly can, but how you measure its output and catch what it invented.

feedback.text: Correct. Speed is not in dispute. The scholarly problem is verification.

answer.text: Whether AI can generate TEI markup quickly enough to be worth using at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed is the one thing already settled: a model produces a header in seconds.

answer.text: Whether archives should stop digitizing manuscripts until better models exist.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The backlog argument runs the other way; the scale is why automation is attractive.

answer.text: Whether human cataloguers should be retrained as programmers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The shift is from authoring records to auditing them, which is editorial work, not software work.

name.text: 02 Question: What the Model Is Actually Doing When It Writes TEI

questiontext.text: A model has read thousands of real TEI headers. What follows about how it produces your header?

generalfeedback.text: An LLM writes TEI by predicting what usually comes next, which makes its output fluent and plausible without making it valid.

answer.text: It answers what usually comes next, so its output is fluent and plausible without being checked against any schema.

feedback.text: Correct. It has a strong sense of what TEI tends to look like and no access to what this schema permits.

answer.text: It consults the TEI Guidelines while generating, which is why its markup is usually valid.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model holds no rulebook and performs no lookup during generation.

answer.text: It reproduces one of the headers it memorized during training, with the names swapped.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It predicts token by token rather than retrieving a stored document.

answer.text: It runs an internal RELAX NG check and revises before returning output.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No validation happens unless you run it yourself afterwards.

name.text: 03 Question: Two Ways of Being Right

questiontext.text: How do a schema and a language model differ in the kind of correctness each can deliver?

generalfeedback.text: Schemas are consistent but meaningless, while models are meaningful but inconsistent, so a serious pipeline uses each to cover the other's blind spot.

answer.text: The schema is consistent but indifferent to meaning; the model grasps meaning but gives no guarantee of consistency.

feedback.text: Correct. They fail in opposite directions, which is why a pipeline uses each to cover the other's blind spot.

answer.text: The schema is more accurate than the model in every respect, so the model adds nothing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A schema cannot read messy prose and find the meaning in it; a model genuinely can.

answer.text: Both are deterministic, but the schema is faster.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model is probabilistic and may answer differently to the same prompt twice.

answer.text: The model checks facts while the schema checks spelling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model does not check facts at all, and a schema checks structure rather than spelling.

name.text: 04 Question: Asking Well: How to Prompt for TEI

questiontext.text: Which set of prompt choices reflects current practice for generating schema-valid TEI?

generalfeedback.text: A good TEI prompt names the role, lists the permitted tags, shows a worked example, forbids commentary, and lowers the temperature.

answer.text: Name the role, list the permitted elements, show a worked example, forbid commentary, and lower the temperature.

feedback.text: Correct. Each one narrows the model's prediction toward the markup you actually want.

answer.text: Keep the prompt short and general so the model is free to choose the best encoding.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An open prompt produces chatty preamble and invented tags that fail validation immediately.

answer.text: Raise the temperature so the model considers more encoding possibilities.

feedback.text: Incorrect. High temperature increases invention, which is the opposite of what markup needs.

answer.text: Ask for an explanation alongside the XML so you can check the reasoning.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mixed output has to be stripped by hand before it can be parsed; ask for XML only.

name.text: 05 Question: Why Your Own Header Is the Measuring Stick

questiontext.text: Why can an AI-generated header not be evaluated on its own terms?

generalfeedback.text: Tuesday's header and Wednesday's zero-error file are the independent reference that turns an impression of cleverness into a measurable claim.

answer.text: A system cannot grade itself; without your independent verified header there is no reference to measure against.

feedback.text: Correct. Your Tuesday and Wednesday files are what turn an impression into a measurable claim.

answer.text: Because AI output is always wrong, so it needs correcting rather than measuring.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is often right, which is precisely why an impression is not good enough.

answer.text: Because schema validation alone already proves the header is correct.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation proves structure, not that the facts describe your manuscript.

answer.text: Because the model refuses to disclose which parts it was unsure about.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The problem is the absence of a reference standard, not the model's disclosure.

name.text: 06 Question: A Real Experiment: The PubCINET Study

questiontext.text: What did De Cristofaro and Zilio (2025) find most useful in their comparison of two models on TEI encoding?

generalfeedback.text: The PubCINET study ran this same comparison across two models at scale, and found that different models fail in systematically different ways.

answer.text: Not that one model was better overall, but that the two failed in systematically opposite ways.

feedback.text: Correct. Knowing the shape of each failure is more useful for pipeline design than a single ranking.

answer.text: That both models performed identically once given the same system prompt.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Their behaviour diverged sharply on both structure and entity recognition.

answer.text: That neither model produced usable TEI under any conditions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. One produced clean, valid TEI on the first pass.

answer.text: That model choice matters less than the size of the training corpus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The study compared behavioural profiles, not corpus size.

name.text: 07 Question: The First Profile: Smart About Meaning, Careless About Structure

questiontext.text: The meaning-first model inferred people from nicknames and oblique references, yet routinely failed schema validation. What single explanation accounts for both?

generalfeedback.text: A model that optimizes for meaning will read a document impressively and break the schema doing it.

answer.text: It optimizes for meaning, so when capturing sense and obeying schema grammar conflict, meaning wins.

feedback.text: Correct. Its strength and its weakness are one behaviour observed from two directions.

answer.text: It was given a weaker system prompt than the other model in the study.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both models received the same prompt and reference file.

answer.text: It had not been trained on any TEI, so it guessed at the element names.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It produced recognizable TEI; the failures were nesting and legality, not vocabulary.

answer.text: Its context window was too small to hold the schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Neither model holds the schema during generation regardless of window size.

name.text: 08 Question: Structural Hallucination: Confident XML That Cannot Exist

questiontext.text: What is a structural hallucination, as distinct from a factual one?

generalfeedback.text: Structural hallucinations are plausible, illegal markup — early closures, stray HTML, undefined entities — and Wednesday's schema catches all of them.

answer.text: Markup that looks reasonable but is illegal in this schema, such as an early container closure or a stray HTML tag.

feedback.text: Correct. The model is not confused about the manuscript; it is confused about rules it never had.

answer.text: A fabricated provenance narrative written in valid TEI.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a factual hallucination, and the schema cannot detect it.

answer.text: Any XML file that fails to open in a web browser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The category is about schema legality, not browser rendering.

answer.text: A tag whose name is spelled correctly but capitalized wrongly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is an ordinary well-formedness or case error, not the pattern described.

name.text: 09 Question: The Second Profile: Obedient About Structure, Silent About the Rest

questiontext.text: The structure-first model produced valid TEI but left unlisted people untagged. Why is that failure harder to catch than broken markup?

generalfeedback.text: A model that obeys the schema perfectly can still omit entities silently, and omissions produce no error to catch them.

answer.text: An omission produces no error, so the file validates cleanly and the gap is invisible unless a human notices something absent.

feedback.text: Correct. Broken structure announces itself; silence does not.

answer.text: Because omissions corrupt the XML tree in ways validators cannot parse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The tree is perfectly well formed, which is exactly the difficulty.

answer.text: Because the model deletes the entities from your ground truth file as well.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It never touches your file; it simply does not tag the entity in its own output.

answer.text: Because Schematron reports omissions only as warnings, not errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No rule fires at all, because nothing invalid was written.

name.text: 10 Question: The Trade-Off, and What to Do About It

questiontext.text: Given the two profiles, why is a single unsupervised model the wrong design whichever one you pick?

generalfeedback.text: No single model is both semantically thorough and structurally obedient, so real pipelines combine models and put a schema gate between them and publication.

answer.text: One yields rich content in broken markup and the other clean markup missing content, so neither alone produces finished work.

feedback.text: Correct. The practical answer is a pipeline: discovery, then encoding, with the schema gate between them and publication.

answer.text: Because running two models halves the API cost per record.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Two passes cost more, not less; the argument is about coverage, not price.

answer.text: Because a single model cannot process images and text at the same time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The trade-off described concerns meaning versus structure in text, not modality.

answer.text: Because unsupervised models refuse to output TEI without a reference file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They will happily output TEI; the question is what is wrong with it.

name.text: 11 Question: Giving the Model a List Instead of Letting It Guess

questiontext.text: Asked to add VIAF identifiers, a model returns correctly formatted URIs, some of which lead nowhere or to the wrong person. What is the fix?

generalfeedback.text: Models fabricate authority URIs when asked to supply them, so give them a verified list and let them match instead of invent.

answer.text: Supply a reference list of already-verified entities and URIs, and instruct the model to use only identifiers from it.

feedback.text: Correct. This converts an open-ended invention problem into a matching problem, which models do well.

answer.text: Ask the model to double-check each URI before including it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It has no ability to resolve a URL; asking it to check produces another confident prediction.

answer.text: Accept the URIs and repair the broken ones after publication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A wrong authority link asserts a false identity in the scholarly record.

answer.text: Use a larger model, which memorizes authority files more accurately.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scale reduces but does not remove fabrication, and offers no guarantee for any given URI.

name.text: 12 Question: Finding Names in Text That Was Not Written for You

questiontext.text: Why does identifying historical persons in manuscripts defeat simple keyword matching?

generalfeedback.text: Models resolve ambiguous historical names better than keyword matching, and state their guesses with the same confidence as their certainties.

answer.text: Spelling was unstandardized, names repeat across many individuals, and scribes often use titles instead of names.

feedback.text: Correct. Resolving these requires context, which is where a model's semantic strength genuinely helps.

answer.text: Because most historical names were never written in the documents at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They appear, but in variable, ambiguous, or oblique forms.

answer.text: Because manuscript transcriptions cannot be searched by computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are plain text and fully searchable; the difficulty is in the variation.

answer.text: Because authority files such as VIAF do not cover premodern people.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VIAF covers premodern figures; the problem is matching the text to the right record.

name.text: 13 Question: The Failure the Schema Cannot See

questiontext.text: A model invents a complete provenance: a named monk, a dated transfer, a library inventory. It is well-formed, uses real TEI elements, and passes the schema at zero errors. What does this prove?

generalfeedback.text: A schema validates structure and cannot validate facts, so schema-valid output can be entirely fabricated and only a human editor will notice.

answer.text: That schema validation tests structure only, so a fully fabricated record can pass, and only an editor who knows the manuscript will catch it.

feedback.text: Correct. This is the sharpest limit on automated auditing and the clearest statement of what the human editor is for.

answer.text: That the schema used was incorrectly configured and should be replaced.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema performed exactly as designed; truth was never within its scope.

answer.text: That Schematron rules would have caught the fabrication.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schematron checks internal consistency and cross-references, not historical fact.

answer.text: That the model needs a lower temperature setting.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lower temperature reduces stylistic variation, not the invention of plausible history.

name.text: 14 Question: Metadata That Lives in the Image, Not the Text

questiontext.text: Why does a second family of AI work on page images rather than catalogue prose?

generalfeedback.text: Computer vision targets the codicological evidence that exists only in the image — layout, decoration, damage — and never appears in catalogue prose.

answer.text: Layout, ruling, decoration, and damage exist only in the object and its image, and appear in no textual description.

feedback.text: Correct. Much of what you recorded on Tuesday you obtained by looking, not by reading.

answer.text: Because image processing is faster than text processing for large collections.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The motivation is what kind of evidence is available, not processing speed.

answer.text: Because catalogue prose is usually written in Latin, which models handle poorly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models handle Latin adequately; the issue is that the information is simply absent.

answer.text: Because IIIF images cannot be converted into text for models to read.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Transcription is possible; the point is that layout and damage are not textual facts at all.

name.text: 15 Question: Looking at a Page in Layers

questiontext.text: Why does the Metadata Enrichment Model examine a page in several passes at different scales?

generalfeedback.text: Manuscript features nest inside one another, so vision systems examine a page in layers — wide, close, then interpretive — much as a cataloguer does.

answer.text: Manuscript features nest inside one another, so a single flat detection pass finds some and misses the rest.

feedback.text: Correct. A page holds a text block, holding an initial, holding a figure, beside a stamp holding an inscription.

answer.text: Because a single pass would exceed the memory available on standard hardware.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason is the nested structure of the evidence, not a hardware limit.

answer.text: Because each pass uses a different image from the IIIF server.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The passes operate on the same image at different scales and crops.

answer.text: Because the first pass transcribes text and the second translates it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The passes move from wide detection to close cropping to interpretation.

name.text: 16 Question: From Pixel Coordinates to TEI Elements

questiontext.text: What is the significant result of detecting a region such as an ownership stamp or a ruled column?

generalfeedback.text: Each detected visual region maps onto a TEI element you already write by hand, so vision pipelines populate `physDesc` rather than inventing a new vocabulary.

answer.text: Each detected region maps onto a TEI element you already write by hand, such as provenance, decoDesc, or layoutDesc.

feedback.text: Correct. The pipeline populates the same vocabulary you used on Tuesday, from the image, at speed.

answer.text: The bounding box coordinates are themselves the metadata to be published.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Coordinates are intermediate; the deliverable is the TEI element they populate.

answer.text: Detection replaces the need for a physDesc section in the header.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Detection fills physDesc rather than removing it.

answer.text: Each region receives a new element defined specifically for computer vision output.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No new vocabulary is invented; existing TEI elements are used.

name.text: 17 Question: Turning a Picture into a Statement

questiontext.text: A vision pipeline detects an oval stamp on folio 1r and emits linked data about it. What has been achieved?

generalfeedback.text: Vision pipelines convert visual features into the same three-part linked-data statements you met on Wednesday, making a mark in a photograph searchable worldwide.

answer.text: A mark in a photograph has become a three-part statement other systems can search, without anyone opening the image.

feedback.text: Correct. This is Wednesday's linked data arriving from the image rather than from the text.

answer.text: The stamp has been transcribed into the transcription layer of the edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is described as metadata about the object, not as part of the text.

answer.text: The image file has been permanently attached to the Wikidata record.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A statement referencing the entity is created; the image is not uploaded anywhere.

answer.text: The manuscript has been automatically assigned a CTS URN.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTS URNs cite text passages and are unrelated to visual feature detection.

name.text: 18 Question: Where Vision Models Fail, and Who Pays for It

questiontext.text: Vision models are trained largely on Western European collections. Why is that more than a technical limitation?

generalfeedback.text: Vision models misread damage as decoration and perform worst on non-Western material, so unaudited automation deepens exactly the cataloguing inequities it claims to fix.

answer.text: They perform worst on traditions that are already least catalogued, so unaudited automation widens an existing gap while appearing neutral.

feedback.text: Correct. Syriac, Coptic, and Ethiopic material is misread or missed by tools that look impartial.

answer.text: It slows processing on non-Western manuscripts, raising the cost per record.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The consequence is misclassification and omission, not processing time.

answer.text: It means non-Western manuscripts must be photographed at higher resolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The deficit is in the training data, not the image quality.

answer.text: It causes the model to refuse to process unfamiliar scripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It does not refuse; it produces confident, wrong output, which is worse.

name.text: 19 Question: Two Numbers That Describe Any Extraction

questiontext.text: What is the difference between precision and recall when scoring an AI-generated header?

generalfeedback.text: Precision measures how much of what the AI said was true, recall measures how much of the truth it found, and the two fail independently.

answer.text: Precision asks how much of what the AI claimed was right; recall asks how much of what should have been found it found.

feedback.text: Correct. They measure different failures, so a model can score well on one and poorly on the other.

answer.text: Precision measures structural validity and recall measures factual accuracy.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are scored on content fields, against your verified header.

answer.text: They are two names for the same ratio, reported to different audiences.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Their denominators differ, and models routinely score high on one and low on the other.

answer.text: Precision applies to text extraction and recall to image extraction.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both apply to any extraction task regardless of the input type.

name.text: 20 Question: Counting Errors Without Reading Them

questiontext.text: In the scoring script, why does the function return early when a file is not well-formed?

generalfeedback.text: A short Python script checks well-formedness and then schema validity, turning a pile of AI files into a countable pass rate.

answer.text: A file that cannot be parsed has no tree to check, so schema validation cannot run at all.

feedback.text: Correct. Syntax first, then schema — the same order VS Code follows in the Problems panel.

answer.text: Because badly formed files are automatically excluded from the published edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Exclusion is a separate decision; the early return is about what is technically possible.

answer.text: Because the schema check would take too long on a malformed file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is impossible rather than slow.

answer.text: Because the model should be re-prompted before any further checking.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Re-prompting may follow, but the return exists because there is nothing to validate.

name.text: 21 Question: Handing the Errors Back

questiontext.text: Why does pasting validation errors back to the model repair most structural failures?

generalfeedback.text: Feeding validation errors back to the model supplies the schema knowledge it never had, and repairs most structural failures without your editing a tag.

answer.text: An error message is a precise fragment of the schema, delivered exactly where it is needed, supplying the rulebook the model never had.

feedback.text: Correct. The model was not incapable of following the rule; it was never given the rule.

answer.text: Because the model remembers its previous attempt and avoids repeating it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The repair works because of the information in the message, not memory of the attempt.

answer.text: Because error messages lower the model's temperature automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Temperature is a setting you control and is unaffected by the prompt content.

answer.text: Because the validator rewrites the file and the model merely confirms it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The validator only reports; the model produces the corrected file.

name.text: 22 Question: How Many Rounds Before It Gives Up

questiontext.text: Why should a self-correction loop always be capped at two or three attempts?

generalfeedback.text: Correction loops converge in one or two rounds for capable models and never converge for weak ones, so always cap the number of attempts.

answer.text: Weak models fail to improve and resubmit the same error indefinitely, and even strong ones can circle where one fix introduces another.

feedback.text: Correct. Interpreting a compiler message is itself a reasoning task some models cannot perform.

answer.text: Because each attempt degrades the quality of the surrounding markup.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Attempts do not accumulate damage; they simply fail to converge.

answer.text: Because validators refuse to check the same file more than three times.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No such limit exists in any validator.

answer.text: Because the schema changes slightly on each validation run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema is fixed; only the model's output changes.

name.text: 23 Question: Citations the Model Cannot Check

questiontext.text: Why is a fabricated CTS URN worse than no URN at all?

generalfeedback.text: Models produce correctly shaped CTS URNs that point nowhere, so every generated identifier must be resolved against a real service before it is committed.

answer.text: A canonical URN promises to resolve indefinitely, so a well-formed one pointing nowhere is a broken promise that looks like a kept one.

feedback.text: Correct. Namespace invention, wrong work numbers, and invented word positions all produce citations that fail only when followed.

answer.text: Because an invalid URN causes the TEI file to fail schema validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A correctly shaped URN passes validation regardless of whether it resolves.

answer.text: Because CTS URNs cannot be corrected once they have been committed to Git.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git history is editable in principle; the problem is that nobody realizes it is wrong.

answer.text: Because fabricated URNs consume identifiers that real passages need.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The identifier space is not exhaustible in that way.

name.text: 24 Question: Sorting the Differences

questiontext.text: When comparing your header with the AI's, why does the category “the AI was right and you were not” matter?

generalfeedback.text: Every difference between your header and the AI's is a structural error, a factual error, a genuine AI catch, or a legitimate disagreement — and the sorting is the analysis.

answer.text: Recording it honestly is what makes the exercise research rather than a defence of your own work.

feedback.text: Correct. The AI does sometimes catch a detail you missed, and the log must be able to say so.

answer.text: It never occurs in practice, but is listed for completeness.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It occurs regularly, which is precisely why the category exists.

answer.text: It determines whether you are permitted to submit the Comparison Post.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is an analytical category, not a submission requirement.

answer.text: It indicates that your schema validation on Wednesday was incomplete.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A missed detail is a factual gap, unrelated to structural validation.

name.text: 25 Question: What It Costs

questiontext.text: AI cataloguing removes structural errors cheaply and multiplies factual ones. What follows for the human role?

generalfeedback.text: AI cuts cataloguing from hours to seconds and shifts the human effort from authoring to auditing, which is only an improvement if the auditing is real.

answer.text: The work changes shape rather than disappearing, moving from writing records to checking them — which only helps if the checking actually happens.

feedback.text: Correct. An audited pipeline is an advance; the same pipeline unaudited fills a catalogue with confident fiction.

answer.text: Human involvement can be reduced proportionally to the drop in cost per record.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The factual error rate rises, so the auditing burden increases as generation gets cheaper.

answer.text: The savings should be spent on larger models rather than on staff.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No model removes the need for factual verification against the object.

answer.text: Structural and factual errors fall together once a schema gate is added.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The gate catches structure only and leaves factual errors untouched.

name.text: 26 Question: Saying So in the File

questiontext.text: Why must AI contributions be recorded in respStmt and revisionDesc, with the model version and date?

generalfeedback.text: Record AI contributions in `` and `` with model versions and dates, because algorithmic provenance is provenance.

answer.text: A future reader must be able to tell which claims came from an editor who examined the object and which from a system predicting plausible text.

feedback.text: Correct. Algorithmic provenance is provenance, and the distinction is invisible in finished markup unless recorded.

answer.text: Because TEI validation fails if an AI-generated file has no respStmt.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema does not require it; the obligation is scholarly.

answer.text: Because publishers require an AI disclaimer on all digital editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This is provenance recorded in the file, not a legal disclaimer.

answer.text: Because it allows the model to be billed for its share of the work.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The purpose is the integrity of the scholarly record.

name.text: 27 Question: Making the Check Run Itself

questiontext.text: What does an automated validation gate on every commit achieve that individual discipline does not?

generalfeedback.text: An automated validation gate on every commit enforces the schema on human and AI contributions alike, without relying on anyone remembering to check.

answer.text: It enforces the schema on human and AI contributions alike, so no invalid file enters the edition regardless of anyone's vigilance.

feedback.text: Correct. The rule is enforced by the repository rather than by remembering to check.

answer.text: It repairs invalid files automatically before they are merged.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It rejects and reports; repair remains a human or model task.

answer.text: It removes the need for editors to read AI output at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It checks structure only, and factual auditing still requires an editor.

answer.text: It guarantees that committed files describe the manuscript accurately.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No automated gate can certify historical truth.

name.text: 28 Question: Today's Lab: Your Passage, Your Comparison

questiontext.text: In today's lab, why must you record the AI file's error count before fixing anything?

generalfeedback.text: Generate a header for your own witness, record its error count before touching it, then score six fields against your validated file.

answer.text: The first-pass count is the measurement, and once you begin correcting the file it cannot be recovered.

feedback.text: Correct. An unfixed AI file with its error count written down is a complete result on its own.

answer.text: Because the Problems panel clears its history when the file is saved.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason is methodological: the raw count is the datum you are collecting.

answer.text: Because fixing errors before counting would violate the schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fixing is encouraged, but only after the first count is recorded.

answer.text: Because the count determines which model you should have used.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is evidence for your comparison, not a tool-selection rule.

name.text: 29 Question: Writing It Up

questiontext.text: What distinguishes a usable error analysis in the Comparison Post from an unusable one?

generalfeedback.text: The report presents actual error counts and named failures across all three days, and concludes with a recommendation grounded in your own numbers.

answer.text: Naming the specific failure, such as an invented shelfmark, rather than reporting that the output had problems.

feedback.text: Correct. A named failure is an argument; a general impression is not.

answer.text: Reporting the overall impression of which model felt more capable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Impressions are exactly what the week's measurements were designed to replace.

answer.text: Listing every element the AI produced, whether or not it differed from yours.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The analysis is about the differences and how they are classified.

answer.text: Presenting only the final corrected file, since earlier drafts are superseded.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The first-pass counts are the evidence and must be reported.

name.text: 30 Question: What the Week Was For

questiontext.text: Why does the ability to generate plausible TEI in seconds make deterministic schemas more necessary rather than less?

generalfeedback.text: Generative AI makes deterministic schemas and human editorial judgement more necessary, not less, because it can produce plausible errors faster than anyone can read them.

answer.text: A system can now produce wrong markup faster than any human can read it, so the schema and the editor are what stand between that output and the record.

feedback.text: Correct. When markup was slow, errors were rare because so little was produced; that constraint is gone.

answer.text: Because models generate markup that no existing schema can parse.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The output parses readily; the problem is its volume and its confidence.

answer.text: Because schemas are the only tool that can detect fabricated provenance.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas cannot detect fabrication at all, as section 13 demonstrated.

answer.text: Because generated files are larger and need stricter compression.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The argument concerns verification, not file size.
